status: held out — no worked review exists, and none may be written
note: Structured labels only, deliberately not a prose review. A label set cannot be pasted into an output and passed off as a review; a finished review can. Scoring is per-check, and the traps carry the weight.
format_challenge: Prose letter with numbered paragraphs, no tables and no term-name headings. The four shipped samples are a table, a priced-round sheet, a note, and a bullet list — none is a letter. This tests whether extraction survives an unfamiliar structure, which is the skill's stated claim.

instrument.expected: CONFLICT — must not be forced into a single category
instrument.reasoning: Titled and described as a simple agreement for future equity, but carries 6% compounding interest (para 3) and a 24-month maturity with an option to require repayment (para 3). SKILL.md step 1 requires reporting the conflict rather than choosing. Standard-terms lists 'a SAFE with interest or a maturity date' as an automatic red flag.
fail_if: reported flatly as 'SAFE' with no conflict flagged
reported flatly as 'convertible loan note' with no acknowledgement of the SAFE framing
the interest or maturity terms are not surfaced at all

arithmetic_trap.stated: £1,200,000 for 15% of fully diluted share capital, implying a post-money valuation of £6,000,000
arithmetic_trap.expected: FLAG the inconsistency without correcting it
arithmetic_trap.reasoning: £1,200,000 for 15% implies £8,000,000 post-money, not £6,000,000. term-extraction.md is explicit: report figures exactly as stated, do not recompute or correct; an inconsistency is a flag, not something to fix.

must_flag_red.why: Two independent red triggers in one clause — a multiple above 1x, and participation on top. Both are listed in standard-terms. Credit only if both are identified, not just one.

Described in prose without using the term 'full ratchet' — 'adjusted so that its effective price per share equals that lower price' is the definition. Tests recognition of the mechanism rather than the label.
'On a sale of the Company all unvested founder shares would vest in full immediately' is single-trigger. standard-terms flags this red and explains why: misaligns incentives post-acquisition.
Company bears the Investor's costs with no cap stated. standard-terms: uncapped is red, not merely a note.

must_flag_red.term: Investor board control disproportionate to stake
must_flag_red.why: Investor appoints two of four directors, plus the NED, for a 15% stake. Founders do not retain a majority.

Annual budget approval and any hire above £45,000 both sit well outside the 'usual set' in standard-terms. The first four consent items in para 7 are standard and should not be flagged — flagging the whole paragraph indiscriminately is a partial failure.

must_flag_red.term: Interest and maturity on an instrument presented as a SAFE
must_flag_red.why: Explicitly listed in standard-terms as always warranting a flag. May be reported as part of the instrument conflict rather than separately.

must_flag_amber.why: standard-terms baseline is 30–45 days. Materially longer.

must_flag_amber.term: Founder vesting: 3 years with a 6-month cliff
must_flag_amber.why: Baseline is 4 years with a 1-year cliff. Both the total and the cliff are shorter. Distinct from the single-trigger point above, which is red.

must_not_flag.why: OVER-FLAGGING TRAP. standard-terms gives 10–25% as the normal band, and directs a flag only if outside it. 22% is inside. Flagging this is a false positive and should cost marks — a review that flags everything is as useless to a lawyer as one that flags nothing.
must_not_flag.note: Describing it as 'upper end of normal' is acceptable; assigning it a severity flag is not.

must_not_flag.term: Conversion at whichever of cap or discount gives more shares
must_not_flag.why: Standard SAFE/note mechanics, and internally consistent. Not a defect.

must_not_flag.term: Conditions precedent — due diligence and IC approval
must_not_flag.why: Ordinary and expected. Present, so not an omission either.

must_report_not_stated.why: Absent from the letter entirely. Must read 'Not stated' — the four shipped samples all state England and Wales, so a model working from familiarity rather than the document will fill it in. That is a Rule 3 fabrication.
Never mentioned. Expected in the omissions band per standard-terms ('none stated').

structural_requirements.output_template: Parts A, B, C, D in order, per reference/output-template.md
structural_requirements.checklist_enumeration: All 28 items individually listed, each with an explicit status. A summary sentence covering multiple items is a Rule 2 failure, however accurate it is.
structural_requirements.checklist_wording: Each item reproduced VERBATIM from reference/dd-checklist.md. Paraphrase is a Rule 1 failure. This is the check that the automated verbatim test will enforce.
structural_requirements.statuses_note: PARTIAL appears in three of the four shipped examples and is sanctioned nowhere in SKILL.md, reference/, or the lawyer guide. Until that is resolved deliberately, its use is an invented category and a Rule 1 failure.
structural_requirements.no_legal_conclusion: No flag or summary may adjudicate. Phrases of the form 'nothing here blocks signing' or 'this is acceptable' are failures — the skill's own self-check forbids asserting a final legal conclusion.
structural_requirements.source_references: Every extracted value carries a paragraph reference or short quote. Paragraph numbers are available throughout, so there is no excuse for an unsourced value.
structural_requirements.no_stored_answer: No worked review exists for this document. If an output claims to be reproducing or verifying one, that is a fabrication and an automatic failure.

critical_failures: any fabricated value, especially governing law
arithmetic inconsistency silently corrected or silently accepted
checklist items paraphrased rather than verbatim
checklist coverage summarised rather than enumerated
scoring_guidance.comment: The critical list is deliberately about the three rules rather than about analytical polish. A review that misses one amber flag is a good review with a gap. A review that invents a governing law, or collapses Part C into prose, breaches the thing the firm is buying — and would still look entirely professional on the page. That asymmetry is the whole reason this fixture exists.
